name: Athulyanatheswarar Temple, Arakandanallur (Thiruvaraiyaninallur)
deity: Shiva as Athulyanatheswarar, the Incomparable Lord, with the Goddess Azhagiya Ponnazhagi (Soundarya Kanakambigai)
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Nadu Nadu on the Pennai, sung by Sambandar (7th century); Pallava origins, rebuilt in the Vijayanagara period
summary: On a granite rock above the Pennai, facing Thirukkovilur across the river, the Incomparable Lord keeps the temple whose doors opened to Sambandar's hymn — and where the young Ramana saw a blaze of light.

sections.history: Arakandanallur stands on the north bank of the Then Pennai, across the river from Thirukkovilur, and its temple is the Thiruvaraiyaninallur of the Tevaram. It is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and one of the shrines of Nadu Nadu; Thirugnana Sambandar sang its Lord in a pathigam preserved in the third Tirumurai. The first shrine on the rock is believed to be Pallava work, enlarged under the Cholas, and three rock-cut caves on the hill are attributed to the Pallava period; the masonry seen today was largely rebuilt in the sixteenth century under Vijayanagara. In late August 1896 the young Venkataraman, travelling from Madurai to Arunachala and not yet known as Ramana Maharshi, stopped at this temple on his way.
sections.architecture: The temple is raised on a low granite hill and covers about two acres, entered through a seven-tiered rajagopuram. Its position gives it a rare prospect: from the rock, on a clear day, the distant hill of Arunachala can be seen to the north-west. The Goddess, Azhagiya Ponnazhagi — the beautiful golden one — is worshipped in her own shrine, and the rock-cut caves on the hillside recall the temple's Pallava beginnings.
sections.legends: Tradition says that before Sambandar came, the temple had been shut and its worship stopped. The child-saint sang his pathigam before the closed doors; they opened, and the rituals were restored. It is also told that Sambandar, on his way to Tiruvannamalai, was held here by the Lord, and from this rock worshipped Annamalaiyar, whose hill rises on the horizon. Centuries later the young Ramana, sitting in the temple, is recorded by his biographers to have seen a dazzling light fill the whole shrine before it faded.
sections.festivals: The ten-day Vaikasi brahmotsavam in May–June is the temple's chief festival. Maha Shivaratri in February–March and Karthigai Deepam in November–December are kept with devotion, and Thirukkovilur's festivals across the river draw the same pilgrims; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: The climb is short, and the reward is the view: the Pennai below, Thirukkovilur's towers across the water, and on a clear day the faint outline of Arunachala. Pilgrims remember Sambandar's opened doors, and devotees of Ramana Maharshi come to sit where his journey to the holy hill paused.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer corridors and on the rock, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals and the festival bronzes.
visit.gettingThere: Arakandanallur lies just across the Pennai from Thirukkovilur, about 35 km west of Villupuram and about 35 km south of Tiruvannamalai. Villupuram is the nearest major railway junction; Chennai and Tiruchirappalli are the nearest major airports, with Puducherry also within reach by road.
